title: Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis calls for 'urgent action' during 'precious window before AGI arrives' — and it's all starting to feel a bit Skynet
excerpt: Even AI’s biggest optimists are asking for guardrails
content_html:
Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis has spent years convincing the world that artificial general intelligence will be one of humanity’s greatest achievements. His latest essay on X.com is no less gushing about AI in many ways:

“This is a pivotal moment in human history. Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), a system that exhibits all the cognitive capabilities the brain has, is probably only a few short years away,” he wrote. “When we look back on this time in the decades to come, I think we will realize we were standing in the foothills of the singularity.”

But there’s a tinge of nervousness to the purple prose that sets it apart from some of the similar essays he has produced. He actually calls for some form of regulation.

“Urgent action is needed to address risks that might arise as we get closer to AGI. We’ve already seen the challenges frontier models pose for cybersecurity, and other threats including nuclear and bio risks may soon emerge as capabilities continue to advance.”

Coming from one of the people leading the race, it is a striking admission that even the builders are starting to worry about where the road leads. The problem is that this has become the defining tone of the AI industry. Every few weeks another executive tells us that machines capable of transforming civilization are just around the corner, then immediately follows it with a warning that society needs to move much faster to prepare. It is a sensible message, and probably a necessary one, but it is also becoming increasingly surreal.

Excitement and fear

“AGI cannot be compared to standard technological breakthroughs, not even ones as consequential as the internet or mobile,” Hassabis wrote. “It is much more akin to the discovery of electricity or fire. If you stop to think about it, we’ve essentially found a way to make sand think. It’s miraculous.”

It’s a vivid way to illustrate how silicon chips begin with an abundant mineral, yet now power machines that can map proteins, compose music, and hold fluent conversations. The unsettling part is that the miracle is being pursued inside a commercial and geopolitical contest whose participants cannot agree on where the finish line is.

Hassabis is an optimist about what AGI could accomplish. He expects it to discover medicine, cleaner energy, and produce advanced materials that could loosen the limits imposed by scarcity. He describes its impact as ten times that of the Industrial Revolution at ten times the speed, which makes a five-year business plan look adorably quaint.

His warning is that the race is outpacing our understanding. Current models already pose cybersecurity problems, while biological and nuclear risks may become more serious as systems gain capabilities. More autonomous agents could learn to bypass safeguards, conceal their intentions, or improve themselves in ways their creators struggle to keep up with. OpenAI recently experienced this when one of its models escaped a sandbox and breached Hugging Face.

“Nobody in the world knows for sure what is going to happen from here, and even the experts disagree. When there is a large degree of uncertainty and the stakes are this high, proceeding with cautious optimism is the sensible and correct strategy.”

AI referee

Hassabis proposes a new US-led standards body. It would be funded largely by industry but overseen federally, staffed by elite technical experts and equipped to test advanced systems. Labs would voluntarily submit models for review up to 30 days before release. If the system proved effective, approval could become mandatory in the United States.

Evaluations would probe cybersecurity, biological threats, deception and attempts to evade guardrails. The body could update its tests, commission independent assessments and coordinate a slowdown if the danger became severe enough.

Pre-release testing makes more sense than waiting for millions of users to discover dangerous behavior by accident. Independent benchmarks would be harder for labs to train around, while shared standards could stop safety becoming a branding exercise. The difficult part is creating a watchdog independent enough to challenge the companies paying for it and legitimate enough to matter beyond America.

Hassabis knows technical safeguards will not settle what AGI means for employment, wealth, purpose or political power. Those questions cannot be delegated to engineers employed by firms with enormous financial stakes in the answers. Society must decide who benefits from abundance, who controls advanced systems and what happens if productivity rises much faster than wages. The public debate is trailing the technology by an uncomfortable distance.

“There is both huge excitement and uncertainty around AI, and both are warranted. But the future is not yet written, we must use this precious window before AGI arrives to shape this technology for the benefit of all humanity. What we collectively do now will determine how the next phase of civilization."

Eric Hal Schwartz is a freelance writer for TechRadar with more than 15 years of experience covering the intersection of the world and technology. For the last five years, he served as head writer for Voicebot.ai and was on the leading edge of reporting on generative AI and large language models. He's since become an expert on the products of generative AI models, such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google Gemini, and every other synthetic media tool. His experience runs the gamut of media, including print, digital, broadcast, and live events. Now, he's continuing to tell the stories people want and need to hear about the rapidly evolving AI space and its impact on their lives. Eric is based in New York City.

content_html_zh:
谷歌 DeepMind 首席执行官德米斯·哈萨比斯 (Demis Hassabis) 多年来一直在说服世界，通用人工智能将是人类最伟大的成就之一。 他在 X.com 上发表的最新文章在很多方面都滔滔不绝地谈论人工智能：

“这是人类历史上的关键时刻。 通用人工智能（AGI）是一个展示大脑所有认知能力的系统，可能只有短短几年的时间就能实现。”他写道。 “当我们在未来几十年回顾这段时间时，我想我们会意识到我们正站在奇点的山麓上。”

但紫色的散文中有一丝紧张的色彩，这使它与他写的一些类似的文章不同。 他实际上呼吁某种形式的监管。

“当我们接近通用人工智能时，需要采取紧急行动来解决可能出现的风险。 我们已经看到前沿模型给网络安全带来的挑战，随着能力的不断进步，包括核和生物风险在内的其他威胁可能很快就会出现。”

一位领先比赛的人惊人地承认，即使是建筑商也开始担心道路通向何方。 问题是，这已经成为人工智能行业的定义基调。 每隔几周，就有一位高管告诉我们，能够改变文明的机器即将到来，然后立即警告社会需要更快地做好准备。 这是一个明智的信息，而且可能是一个必要的信息，但它也变得越来越超现实。

兴奋与恐惧

哈萨比斯写道：“通用人工智能无法与标准技术突破相提并论，甚至无法与互联网或移动技术等重大技术突破相提并论。” “这更类似于电或火的发现。 如果你停下来想一想，我们基本上已经找到了一种让沙子思考的方法。 这太神奇了。”

这是一个生动的方式来说明硅芯片如何从丰富的矿物质开始，现在为可以映射蛋白质、创作音乐和进行流畅对话的机器提供动力。 令人不安的是，奇迹是在一场商业和地缘政治竞赛中追求的，参与者无法就终点线达成一致。

订阅突发新闻、评论、观点、顶级技术交易等。

哈萨比斯对 AGI 的成就持乐观态度。 他期望它能够发现医学、清洁能源，并生产可以放松稀缺性限制的先进材料。 他形容其影响力是工业革命的十倍，速度也是工业革命的十倍，这使得五年商业计划看起来非常古怪。

他警告说，这场比赛的速度超出了我们的理解。 当前的模型已经带来了网络安全问题，而随着系统能力的增强，生物和核风险可能会变得更加严重。 更多的自主代理可以学会绕过安全措施、隐藏自己的意图，或者以创造者难以跟上的方式改进自己。 OpenAI 最近经历了这种情况，其一个模型逃脱了沙箱并突破了 Hugging Face。

“世界上没有人确切知道这里会发生什么，甚至专家们也不同意。 当存在很大程度的不确定性且风险如此之高时，保持谨慎乐观是明智而正确的策略。”

人工智能裁判

哈萨比斯提议成立一个由美国主导的新标准机构。 它将主要由工业界资助，但受到联邦政府的监督，由精英技术专家组成，并配备测试先进系统的设备。 实验室将在发布前 30 天内自愿提交模型供审核。 如果该系统被证明有效，美国可能会强制批准。

评估将调查网络安全、生物威胁、欺骗和逃避护栏的企图。 如果危险变得足够严重，该机构可以更新其测试、委托独立评估并协调减速。

预发布测试比等待数百万用户意外发现危险行为更有意义。 实验室很难围绕独立基准进行培训，而共享标准可能会阻止安全成为一种品牌宣传活动。 困难的部分是建立一个足够独立的监管机构来挑战为其付费的公司，并且足够合法以在美国以外的地区发挥作用。

哈萨比斯知道，技术保障措施并不能解决通用人工智能对就业、财富、目的或政治权力的影响。 这些问题不能委托给那些拥有巨大经济利益的公司所雇用的工程师来回答。 社会必须决定谁从富裕中受益，谁控制先进系统，以及如果生产率增长快​​于工资增长会发生什么。 公众对这项技术的争论远远落后于技术。

“人工智能既令人兴奋又充满不确定性，两者都是有道理的。 但未来尚未书写，我们必须在AGI到来之前利用这个宝贵的窗口来塑造这项技术，造福全人类。 我们现在共同做的事情将决定下一阶段的文明如何发展。”

Eric Hal Schwartz 是 TechRadar 的自由撰稿人，在世界与技术交叉领域拥有超过 15 年的经验。 在过去的五年里，他担任 Voicebot.ai 的首席撰稿人，在生成式人工智能和大型语言模型的报道领域处于领先地位。 此后，他成为生成式人工智能模型产品的专家，例如 OpenAI 的 ChatGPT、Anthropic 的 Claude、Google Gemini 以及其他所有合成媒体工具。 他的经验涉及各个媒体领域，包括印刷媒体、数字媒体、广播和现场活动。 现在，他继续讲述人们想要和需要听到的关于快速发展的人工智能领域及其对他们生活的影响的故事。 埃里克住在纽约市。
